Reasons and Justifications:

  • Ambiguity in International Law: Some argue that existing international space law, particularly the Outer Space Treaty of 1967, is ambiguous regarding resource extraction. Without the guarantee of ownership and the ability to profit from space resources, companies may be hesitant to invest the significant capital required. A unilateral approach, in their view, provides that clarity and spurs innovation more rapidly than protracted international negotiations.

  • Extended Space Exploration: In-situ resource utilization (ISRU) could make long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and other destinations more sustainable and affordable.   • Ethical Considerations: The potential for commercial exploitation of space resources raises ethical questions about the equitable distribution of benefits and the preservation of space environments for future generations.

The idea of the US pursuing unilateral space resource exploitation is driven by a desire for economic growth, technological leadership, and national security. However, it is fraught with legal, ethical, and practical challenges. It could potentially lead to international conflict, undermine existing international agreements, and raise concerns about environmental protection. A multilateral approach, despite being slower and more complex, is generally seen as a more sustainable and responsible path forward for space resource utilization.

It is important to stay informed about ongoing discussions within the United Nations and other international forums about the development of a legal framework for space resource activities. The Case for American Leadership in Space: Unilateral Exploitation of Lunar, Martian, and Asteroidal Resources

Introduction

The dawn of the 21st century has brought humanity to the precipice of a new frontier: the vast, untapped wealth of the solar system. The Moon, Mars, and nearby asteroids hold immense reserves of rare minerals, precious metals, and volatile compounds essential for both economic prosperity and national security. Yet, despite the promise of this celestial bonanza, the United States remains shackled by outdated international treaties that treat space as a commons, denying individual nations the right to claim and develop these vital resources. The Outer Space Treaty (OST) of 1967, while noble in its intent to prevent conflict and militarization, was drafted in an era when space was the sole domain of superpower rivalry, not commercial enterprise. Today, the legal ambiguities of the OST—particularly its prohibition on national sovereignty while remaining silent on resource extraction—present the United States with a historic opportunity: to embrace a bold, visionary policy of unilateral exploitation of off-world resources for the betterment of its economy and security.

Rather than waiting for sluggish international consensus or ceding the initiative to rivals like China, which has already outlined aggressive plans for lunar and asteroid mining, the United States must act decisively. By unilaterally claiming and exploiting the Moon’s helium-3 reserves, Mars’ strategic metals, and the trillion-dollar asteroid belt, America can secure economic dominance, reduce its dependence on foreign supply chains, and ensure its position as the preeminent spacefaring power. This essay argues that the benefits—both economic and strategic—of such a policy far outweigh the perceived legal and diplomatic risks, and that the time for action is now.

Economic Supremacy Through Space Resource Exploitation

The economic case for U.S. unilateral exploitation of extraterrestrial resources is overwhelming. Analyses by organizations such as the U.S. Geological Survey, Goldman Sachs, and the Colorado School of Mines estimate that a single metallic asteroid could contain more platinum-group metals than have ever been mined on Earth—valued in the trillions of dollars. The Moon alone holds an estimated 1.1 million tons of helium-3, a clean-burning isotope that could revolutionize fusion energy, potentially solving global energy shortages while positioning the U.S. as the leader in next-generation power technology. Water ice, abundant in lunar polar craters, can be refined into hydrogen and oxygen for rocket fuel, drastically reducing the cost of deep-space missions and enabling the U.S. to dominate cislunar commerce.

Creating a Trillion-Dollar Space Economy

By leading in resource extraction, the United States can catalyze a new economic paradigm. The commercial space sector is projected to grow from $400 billion today to over $1 trillion by 2040, according to Bank of America. Companies like SpaceX, Blue Origin, and AstroForge are already investing heavily in asteroid mining technology, with AstroForge announcing plans to launch its first prospecting mission in 2025. If the U.S. establishes legal precedent for resource ownership—through domestic legislation like the Space Act of 2015 (which grants U.S. companies rights to extracted asteroidal resources)—it can attract private investment, spur innovation, and create millions of high-skills jobs in aerospace, robotics, and advanced manufacturing.

Moreover, space-based industries could reduce America’s dependency on foreign supply chains for critical minerals like cobalt, rare earth elements, and platinum, which are currently dominated by China. A 2022 U.S. Department of Defense report warned that China’s control over 80% of global rare earth production poses a critical national security risk. By mining these resources in space, the U.S. could secure its own supply, stabilizing industries from defense to clean energy. This economic self-sufficiency would not only strengthen America’s industrial base but also generate substantial royalty revenues and export markets, further boosting GDP.

Avoiding the Tragedy of the Commons in Space

Critics argue that unregulated extraction could lead to over-exploitation, much like the environmental degradation seen on Earth. However, space is not Earth—there is no fragile ecosystem to destroy, and the scale of mining required to disrupt celestial bodies is far beyond current capabilities. Furthermore, the U.S. could establish sustainable mining practices by partnering with private industry to create international norms (such as those in the Artemis Accords) that promote responsible exploitation. If America does not take the lead, other nations—particularly China—will fill the void. In 2021, China landed a rover on the Moon’s far side and has since discussed lunar mining for helium-3. If the U.S. hesitates, it risks ceding economic primacy in the final frontier.

National Security Imperatives in the Space Age

While the economic stakes are enormous, the strategic implications of failing to secure off-world resources are even more dire. The 2022 U.S. Space Force Chief of Space Operations Gen. John Raymond warned that space is no longer just a contested domain—it is a warfighting domain, and control over resources will determine who sets the rules for future conflict. The U.S. cannot afford to rely on treaties that non-adherent nations like China and Russia ignore; it must secure its interests unilaterally.

Preventing Resource Monopolies by Adversaries

China’s 2021 white paper on space explicitly states its intention to "explore and utilize lunar and asteroid resources to support sustainable development." Meanwhile, Russia has revived its Soviet-era space ambitions, with Roscosmos planning lunar bases by the 2030s. If either power establishes dominance over helium-3, platinum, or other high-value resources, it could dictate terms to the rest of the world, much like OPEC did with oil in the 20th century. The United States cannot allow a space OPEC to emerge where economic coercion becomes a geopolitical weapon.

A unilateral U.S. approach would allow America to control supply chains and pricing for resources that will be vital to future technology. For example:

  • Helium-3 (³He) from the Moon could power fusion reactors, giving the U.S. energy independence while denying competitors this resource.
  • Water ice on the Moon and Mars could be used to produce rocket fuel, enabling the U.S. to establish refueling depots that dominate cislunar and interplanetary trade routes.
  • Rare earth metals from asteroids could break China’s monopoly, ensuring supply for hypersonic missiles, microchips, and renewable energy technology.

Military Advantages of Space Resource Sovereignty

The U.S. military is already the most space-dependent force in history, relying on satellites for GPS, communications, reconnaissance, and missile guidance. By securing extraterrestrial resources, the U.S. could:

  • Reduce launch costs by manufacturing propellant on the Moon or in orbit, allowing faster deployment of assets during crises.
  • Develop in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) technology to support lunar and Martian bases, ensuring that troops and equipment can be sustained without vulnerable supply lines.
  • Deny adversaries the ability to disrupt U.S. space operations by controlling key resource nodes (e.g., fuel depots that enemy missiles cannot easily target without escalating conflict).

The U.S. must not repeat the mistakes of the past, where over-reliance on foreign supply chains (e.g., semiconductor manufacturing in Taiwan) left the nation vulnerable. Space resources are the ultimate strategic reserve—and America must claim them before others do.

Legal and Strategic Justification for Unilateral Action

The primary objection to this proposal will come from those who argue that the Outer Space Treaty (OST) prohibits national appropriation of space resources. However, this interpretation is legally and morally untenable in the context of modern space development.

The OST’s Ambiguities Work in America’s Favor

Article II of the OST states that "outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty." However, it does not explicitly prohibit resource extraction—only sovereign claims over celestial bodies. This critical distinction means that:

  • A country cannot claim the Moon as its territory, but it can own what it extracts.
  • The U.S. Space Act of 2015 and the Artemis Accords (2020), signed by 40+ nations, already recognize commercial rights to space resources—undermining the claim that the OST prohibits extraction.

The same principle applies in space. If the U.S. begins mining helium-3 on the Moon or extracting platinum from an asteroid, it creates a new legal reality—one that the international community will be forced to accept or ignore at its peril.

Addressing Counterarguments

1. "This Violates International Law"

Rebuttal: The OST’s restrictions on sovereignty do not apply to resource extraction. The U.S. is not claiming the Moon as American soil—it is securing the rights to what it legally extracts, much like a fisherman owns the fish he catches in international waters. The Artemis Accords already provide a legal framework that over 40 nations have endorsed, proving that resource rights are gaining acceptance.

2. "This Could Trigger an Arms Race in Space"

Rebuttal: The U.S. is not militarizing space—it is securing economic and security interests that ensure its dominance. China and Russia are already developing anti-satellite weapons and lunar military bases. By controlling resources, the U.S. ensures it has the financial and logistical capacity to respond to threats without resorting to conflict. A strong economy in space makes deterrence more credible.

3. "Space Mining Will Deplete Resources and Harm the Environment"

Rebuttal: Unlike Earth, space is a vacuum with no biosphere to disrupt. Helium-3 mining on the Moon, for example, would remove only minute quantities compared to the scale of available resources. Furthermore, in-situ utilization (using mined materials locally) reduces the need for Earth launches, decreasing pollution. The U.S. can—and should—establish sustainability guidelines to ensure responsible exploitation.

4. "Other Nations Will Protest and Isolate the U.S."

Rebuttal: Diplomatic protests from non-aligned nations (e.g., Russia, China, or a few smaller states) will carry no legal weight if the U.S. acts within the bounds of emerging international norms (e.g., Artemis Accords). The rest of the world depends on U.S. technology, investment, and security guarantees—if nations want access to American space infrastructure, they will have no choice but to acquiesce to U.S.-dominated resource rights.

Conclusion: America Must Lead, or Be Left Behind

The choice before the United States is stark: act boldly to secure the economic and strategic future of the free world in space, or retreat into passivity while rivals like China and Russia carve up the solar system for their own benefit. The Outer Space Treaty, written in an era of Cold War rivalry, was never meant to govern a commercial space economy—and its ambiguities must not be allowed to strangle American progress.

The benefits of unilateral exploitation are too vast to ignore:

  • Economic dominance through trillions in new industries, jobs, and resource independence.
  • National security supremacy by denying adversaries control over critical materials and securing U.S. supply chains.
  • Geopolitical leverage by setting the legal and economic standards for space commerce.

History will remember those who had the vision to embrace a new frontier and the resolve to secure it. The Moon, Mars, and the asteroid belt are humanity’s next great economic and military frontiers. The United States, as the world’s leading democracy and protector of free enterprise, has both the moral and strategic duty to claim its rightful place as the first and greatest spacefaring nation.

The time to act is now. The resources are there. The technology is within reach. The only question is whether America will lead—or be led by those who are unafraid to seize the initiative.

The choice is clear. Let us choose to lead.

The Case for Unilateral Exploitation: Economic and Security Imperatives

By moving forward unilaterally, the U.S. could establish "facts on the ground" (or in space), creating a de facto legal regime based on customary use and prior appropriation, which proponents argue is a more practical and effective way to govern frontier expansion.

The Case for Multilateral Governance: Diplomacy, Equity, and Stability

Conversely, opponents of unilateral exploitation argue that disregarding international treaties in favor of unilateral resource extraction would be a profound strategic miscalculation, carrying severe diplomatic, legal, and long-term security risks.

Geopolitical Stability and the Rules-Based Order Critics emphasize that the Outer Space Treaty has successfully prevented the weaponization and territorialization of space for over half a century. Introduction

Space Resources Are a Strategic Economic Opportunity

Human civilization has repeatedly been transformed by access to new frontiers and new resources. Maritime trade routes, petroleum fields, railroads, telecommunications networks, and the digital economy all created immense wealth for countries that invested early and built the institutions needed to sustain leadership. The United States should strengthen this framework. It should establish a transparent licensing process for resource operations, safety zones around active equipment, environmental and heritage protections, reporting requirements, dispute-resolution mechanisms, and standards for preventing harmful interference. These measures would not be claims of sovereignty over territory. They would be practical rules enabling operators to work safely and responsibly.

At the same time, Washington should build international coalitions around these principles. The Artemis Accords provide a useful starting point by encouraging transparency, interoperability, emergency assistance, registration of space objects, and responsible resource use. The United States should expand such partnerships, particularly with allies that possess advanced scientific, industrial, and legal capabilities.

Private enterprise will be the engine of large-scale space development. Government can fund research, establish national goals, and provide strategic infrastructure, but commercial firms are more likely to innovate rapidly, reduce costs, and discover viable business models.

  1. Long-term lunar infrastructure contracts. NASA and other agencies should purchase transportation, communications, power, construction, and resource-delivery services from American firms.   2. Clear resource-rights legislation. Congress should clarify that American operators may possess, use, transfer, and sell lawfully extracted extraterrestrial resources, while requiring compliance with safety, environmental, and transparency standards.

  3. Investment incentives. Tax credits, research grants, loan guarantees, and insurance mechanisms could help early-stage companies overcome the high cost and uncertainty of space-resource missions.

  4. Technology protection. The United States must prevent sensitive technologies from being transferred to strategic competitors through theft, coercion, investment schemes, or poorly regulated partnerships.

  5. Strategic stockpiling and procurement. The federal government should be prepared to buy certain space-derived products and services—such as lunar water, propellant, or construction materials—when doing so supports national-security objectives.

  6. Workforce development. Universities, technical schools, and national laboratories should expand programs in robotics, planetary science, aerospace engineering, autonomous systems, nuclear power, materials science, and space law.

Scientific research must remain possible. Activities that create dangerous debris, contaminate sensitive regions, or interfere with other missions should be prohibited.

These constraints are not weaknesses. They strengthen the legitimacy and durability of U.S. leadership. A system that rewards investment while demanding transparency, safety, and environmental stewardship will attract partners and reduce the risk of conflict.

The alternative is not a romantic world in which space remains untouched forever. Other nations will pursue space resources, and technological progress will make extraction increasingly feasible. The real choice is whether the rules will be shaped by open societies with accountable institutions or by states willing to use secrecy, coercion, and strategic dependency to expand their power.

The United States should not surrender the economic and strategic future of space to hesitation. The Moon, Mars, and asteroids represent a new domain of opportunity, and American leadership in that domain can strengthen the nation’s prosperity, security, technological capacity, and global influence.

The proper objective is not reckless annexation or disregard for international obligations. It is confident, lawful, and strategically ambitious leadership: protecting the rights of American innovators, building the infrastructure of a space-based economy, preventing coercive domination by rivals, and forging practical international rules that reward responsible development.

If the United States acts decisively now, it can help ensure that the emerging space-resources economy reflects openness, innovation, security, and the rule of law—while preserving America’s ability to prosper and remain secure in the century ahead.

The strongest unilateralist case is built around first-mover advantages.

  1. Secure commercially viable sites before competitors do.
  2. Create legal certainty for domestic companies.
  3. Attract capital, talent, and foreign partners to U.S. firms.
  4. Build the infrastructure on which later space commerce depends.

Thus, the pro-unilateral case emphasizes speed, investment incentives, strategic access, and leadership. The opposing case stresses legality, legitimacy, long-term stability, environmental protection, and the risk that a scramble for space resources could make future exploration more dangerous and less cooperative.

The Case for Unilateral American Sovereignty Over Lunar, Martian, and Asteroidal Resources: A National Imperative

Introduction

The Moon, Mars, and the asteroid belt represent the next frontier of human ambition—a vast reservoir of rare minerals, water ice, and energy sources that could revolutionize Earth’s economy and security. Yet, despite the overwhelming potential of these celestial bodies, the United States remains constrained by outdated international treaties, particularly the Outer Space Treaty (1967), which declares space as the "province of all mankind." This essay argues that the U.S. should ignore the Outer Space Treaty’s prohibitions on territorial claims, instead adopting a realpolitik approach to secure its rightful place as the leader of space exploration and resource extraction. The economic benefits—from rare earth metals to helium-3 fusion fuel—are too vast to ignore, while the strategic advantages—from energy independence to military superiority—are non-negotiable. The time for hesitation is over; the United States must act decisively to ensure its survival and prosperity in a post-Earth economy.

I. The Economic Imperative: A Trillion-Dollar Opportunity

A. The Value of Lunar and Asteroidal Resources

The Moon alone contains billions of tons of helium-3, a rare isotope that could enable clean, limitless fusion energy—potentially ending Earth’s dependence on fossil fuels. A single kilogram of helium-3 could power a city for a year. Additionally, the Moon’s regolith contains platinum-group metals (PGMs), rare earth elements (REEs), and aluminum, which are critical for modern technology, defense, and renewable energy.

Asteroids are even more valuable. Near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) contain metals worth trillions—some, like 16 Psyche, are composed almost entirely of iron, nickel, and gold, with an estimated value of $10,000 quadrillion (more than the entire global economy). Extracting even a fraction of these resources could eliminate Earth’s mineral scarcity crises, reducing reliance on China and other adversaries for critical supplies.

B. The Cost of Inaction: Losing the Race to Space Capitalism

If the U.S. does not act unilaterally, it risks losing the economic lead to China, Russia, and private corporations. China has already launched missions to the Moon and Mars, with plans to establish a lunar base by 2030. If Beijing secures these resources first, it could dominate global supply chains, making the U.S. dependent on Chinese space minerals—just as it is today with rare earths.

Private companies like AstroForge, Planetary Resources, and SpaceX are already positioning themselves to mine asteroids. If the U.S. does not legally and militarily secure its rights, these firms may operate under foreign jurisdiction, allowing China or Russia to tax or block American access to these resources.

C. The Fiscal and Industrial Benefits of Space Exploitation

A U.S.-led space mining industry would:

  • Create millions of high-paying jobs in aerospace, robotics, and energy.
  • Reduce inflation by securing stable supplies of critical minerals.
  • Stimulate innovation in fusion energy, propulsion, and manufacturing.

II. The National Security Imperative: Dominance in the New Space Age

A. Energy Independence Through Fusion and Propellant Production

Helium-3 from the Moon could replace nuclear fission, eliminating the need for uranium and reducing proliferation risks. Additionally, water ice on the Moon and Mars can be split into hydrogen and oxygen, providing propellant for deep-space missions—giving the U.S. unmatched military and commercial reach.

If the U.S. controls these resources, it can deny them to adversaries, forcing China and Russia to rely on Earth-based supplies—making their economies more vulnerable to sanctions and supply chain disruptions.

B. Military Superiority in Space and Beyond

The U.S. must control the high ground—literally. A lunar or Martian military presence would allow:

  • Uninterruptible satellite communications (no risk of jamming or kinetic strikes).
  • Advanced sensor networks for early warning of missile launches.
  • Off-world staging grounds for rapid deployment of troops or assets.

China’s space force (PLASF) and Russia’s military space program are expanding rapidly. If the U.S. does not assert dominance in space, it risks losing its strategic edge—just as it did in the 20th century with nuclear weapons and now with semiconductor technology.

C. Preventing Adversarial Exploitation of Space Resources

China has explicitly stated its intention to use space resources for military purposes. If Beijing secures lunar helium-3, it could develop fusion weapons or energy-based directed-energy weapons, threatening U.S. security. The U.S. must preemptively secure its rights before adversaries do.

A. The Treaty’s Flaws and Enforcement Gaps

The Outer Space Treaty (1967) prohibits national appropriation of celestial bodies, but it also does not prevent private or corporate exploitation—only government claims. However, the treaty’s weak enforcement means it is easily circumvented.

  • The Monroe Doctrine (1823) – America’s right to intervene in the Western Hemisphere.
  • The U.S. occupation of Hawaii and Puerto Rico – Defied international norms for strategic gain.
  • The U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Climate Accord (2017) – Prioritized economic interests over global consensus.

The U.S. is the world’s largest economy, most advanced military, and leader in space exploration. It has a moral obligation to secure its future—not to cede it to authoritarian regimes.

The Outer Space Treaty was written in an era when space was a Cold War battleground, not an economic frontier. Today, realpolitik demands real action. The United States must unilaterally claim and exploit these resources, ensuring that America remains the leader of the next industrial revolution.

Delay is suicide. The time to act is now.

These are not speculative fantasies; they are tangible assets of incalculable value, lying dormant while terrestrial economies stagnate under debt and resource constraints. The current treaty framework, which prohibits any nation from claiming sovereignty, effectively places a "No Trespassing" sign on the greatest economic frontier in human history. American companies, backed by the full force of U.S. law and guaranteed property rights, would flood the void, triggering a resource boom that would dwarf the Gilded Age. China understands this; it has already begun planning its own lunar resource exploitation under a model of state-corporate nationalism. The Legal Framework and Interpretation

The cornerstone of space law is the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. Article I of the Treaty states that the exploration and use of outer space shall be carried out for the benefit and in the interests of all countries and that space shall be the "province of all mankind." Building on this interpretation, the United States passed the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015. The development of a space-based mining industry could diversify global supply chains. Proponents argue that a U.S.-led space economy would ensure access to these materials without relying on potential adversaries.

Beyond economics, proponents emphasize the strategic necessity of maintaining a dominant presence in space, framing resource control as a matter of national security.

1. Freedom of Action: In a military sense, a nation that can sustain operations in space without constant supply lines from Earth gains a distinct advantage. Control over fuel and materials ensures long-term presence and operational continuity. 2. Deterrence and Leadership: A strong presence in the lunar and asteroid markets serves as a demonstration of capability. Supporters argue that by establishing a lead in space utilization, the U.S. sets the standards for space operations. This includes the ability to enforce norms that favor peaceful use and U.S. commercial interests. Counter-Arguments and International Implications

While the arguments for U.S. exploitation focus on opportunity and security, they exist in tension with the "province of all mankind" clause of the Outer Space Treaty.

1. Global Equity: Critics argue that allowing a single nation to appropriate resources concentrates wealth and technological power in the hands of a few, exacerbating the global development gap. Conclusion

The question of space resource utilization is not merely about technical capability; it is about the future governance of the space domain. The arguments for the United States to pursue resource exploitation are rooted in legitimate economic and national security interests. They emphasize the need for innovation, energy independence, and the preservation of strategic advantages in an increasingly competitive environment.

However, these arguments must be weighed against the long-term value of international cooperation and legal stability. A successful space strategy likely involves a dual approach: asserting the right to utilize resources to drive innovation and security while engaging diplomatically to establish rules that prevent conflict and ensure equitable access. While the U.S. maintains that its current laws are compatible with the Outer Space Treaty, the path forward requires a balance between national ambition and the shared interest of humanity in the cosmos.

Here is a detailed persuasive essay arguing in favor of the United States unilaterally claiming and exploiting space resources.

The Final Frontier Is Ours: Why America Must Claim Space Resources Now

For too long, the United States has operated in space under a self-imposed straitjacket of outdated international agreements, most notably the 1967 Outer Space Treaty (OST). This treaty, crafted in the middle of the Cold War by nations with no capacity to reach the stars, declared space the "province of all mankind" and prohibited national appropriation of celestial bodies. This language is a relic of a bipolar world, a philosophical nicety rendered obsolete by the realities of the 21st-century global economy and the resumption of great-power competition. To ensure its economic prosperity and national security, the United States must unilaterally claim ownership of and exploit the vast resources of the Moon, Mars, and asteroids, even if it means disregarding these outdated international constraints.

The first and most compelling argument is economic. The potential wealth contained in near-Earth asteroids alone is staggering—a single metallic asteroid, such as 16 Psyche, contains enough iron, nickel, and precious metals to be valued in the quintillions of dollars. The Moon holds vast deposits of Helium-3, a potential fuel for clean fusion energy, as well as water ice that can be converted into rocket propellant. By unilaterally claiming these resources, the United States would secure a definitive economic advantage over every other nation on Earth for generations. A new space economy, driven by American enterprise, would create millions of high-paying jobs, spawn transformative technologies with terrestrial applications, and inject trillions of dollars into the U.S. economy. Waiting for a global consensus on resource rights is economic suicide. While the U.S. dithers, China is actively building its own lunar bases and signing bilateral resource-sharing agreements with allied states like Russia. The race to dominate the space economy is on, and the only way to win is to seize the assets first.

Equally critical is the national security imperative. Control of space is control of the Earth. In an era where warfare is increasingly conducted through satellites—from GPS-guided munitions to reconnaissance and communications—whoever controls the cislunar economy controls the high ground of global conflict. Heavy industry in space, powered by lunar and asteroid resources, would allow the United States to construct, repair, and resupply its orbital assets without relying on vulnerable terrestrial launches. Furthermore, establishing an American presence with absolute property rights on the Moon and Mars creates permanent strategic outposts that cannot be challenged. If the U.S. does not claim and militarize these territories, an adversary will. A unilateral claim backed by American technological prowess and, if necessary, military force, will deter rivals and ensure that no hostile power gains a foothold from which to threaten the homeland. The OST’s restriction on sovereignty serves no purpose if a rival state decides to ignore it—and they will. The United States must lead, not follow, in establishing a new doctrine of space sovereignty.

Detractors will argue that disregarding the Outer Space Treaty will undermine the international rule of law and trigger a costly space arms race. This argument is naive and defeatist. The OST is fundamentally unenforceable and has already been rendered moot by subsequent practice. The 1979 Moon Agreement, which would have established a "Common Heritage of Mankind" framework, was signed by only a handful of nations and never ratified by any major spacefaring power. The late, lamented 2015 U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act already allows American companies to own resources they extract from space, which technically conflicts with the OST’s prohibition on national appropriation. The "rule of law" has already been broken; the U.S. merely needs to codify the next logical step of full territorial claim.

Moreover, the concept of "province of all mankind" is a socialist fantasy that would destroy incentivization. If all nations share the bounty of space equally, then no nation has an incentive to invest the enormous capital required for extraction. Who would finance a multi-billion-dollar mission to mine an asteroid if the resulting profit had to be distributed to every nation on Earth, including those who made no investment but are ruled by hostile regimes? This is not magnanimity; it is a recipe for stagnation and poverty. A unilateral American claim is morally defensible precisely because it rewards innovation, risk, and hard work. It adheres to the Lockean principle that property is created through the application of labor and capital to unowned resources. The Moon and Mars are not "owned" by humanity; they are unowned. The first nation to successfully develop and exploit them has the natural right to claim them.

Finally, the strategic timing demands action. The window of American dominance is closing. China's Chang'e missions have landed on the far side of the Moon and returned samples, and their plans for an International Lunar Research Station are proceeding at a breakneck pace. If the United States adheres to a 1960s legal framework while China occupies the most valuable lunar water-ice craters and the most efficient asteroid orbits, the cost to American security will be catastrophic and irreversible. The United States should unilaterally declare its sovereignty over the Moon’s south pole, claim strategic asteroid belts, and begin immediate extraction operations under the authority of a new "Space Territorial Act." The UN will object, rivals will protest, but in the end, possession is nine-tenths of the law—especially in a lawless frontier.

The call to disregard the Outer Space Treaty is not a call for chaos, but a call for a new, honest, and enforceable order rooted in American strength. The U.S. has an unprecedented opportunity to usher in a new era of abundance and security for its citizens. It must not squander it to appease nations that have never launched a rocket and will never contribute a dollar to space development. The first law of the universe is survival, and the second is ownership. America must boldly claim its future among the stars. Failure to do so is not peace; it is surrender.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of the United States pursuing unilateral appropriation and exploitation of space resources from the Moon, Mars, and asteroids without regard for current international space agreements, focusing on advantages in economic growth, technological leadership, and national interests.
Model Response:

The idea of the United States pursuing unilateral exploitation of space resources—Moon, Mars, asteroids—outside the framework of current international agreements is a matter of intense debate. Proponents of such a strategy argue that the existing treaties, especially the 1967 Outer Space Treaty (OST), are ambiguous, outdated, and increasingly ill-suited to the realities of commercial space activity. While this approach is legally and diplomatically contested, advocates identify several key reasons and supposed benefits, particularly in economic growth, technological leadership, and national interests.

1. Economic Growth and the Creation of a Space Economy

The most prominent argument for unilateral resource appropriation is the potential for enormous economic returns.

Access to Trillion-Dollar Resources

Asteroids are known to contain vast quantities of platinum-group metals, nickel, iron, and water. The Moon holds rare-earth elements, titanium, and helium-3—a potential fuel for future fusion reactors. By moving quickly to extract and sell these resources, the United States could effectively create a new industrial sector in space.

Proponents argue that waiting for a global consensus on property rights would only delay this economic opportunity. By asserting the right to extract and own resources unilaterally, the U.S. could give its companies the legal certainty they need to invest billions in space mining. That investment would generate jobs, create new supply chains, and stimulate ancillary industries on Earth—from robotics and AI to launch services and materials science.

Fuel Depots and In-Space Refueling

Water ice from the Moon or asteroids can be split into hydrogen and oxygen—rocket propellant. A U.S.-controlled refueling infrastructure in space would dramatically lower the cost of deep-space missions and open up new commercial markets, including satellite servicing, space tourism, and eventually Mars colonization. This would create a self-sustaining economic ecosystem in cislunar space, with the U.S. as its center.

Revenue from Intellectual Property and Licensing

A unilateral approach would allow U.S. companies and government agencies to define the technical and legal standards for extraction, processing, and transport. If American firms establish the first working space-mining systems, they will hold the patents, proprietary processes, and operational data that other nations would need to license—generating long-term revenue beyond the resources themselves.

2. Technological Leadership and Innovation

Advocates claim that a aggressive, unilateral push into space resource extraction would accelerate American technological dominance in several critical areas.

First-Mover Advantage

One of the strongest arguments is that whoever builds the first operational space-mining and resource-utilization systems will set the global standard. This is comparable to the early space race, where the first lunar landing signaled technological superiority. By moving unilaterally, the U.S. avoids being slowed down by long negotiations and can secure the position of the primary supplier of space-derived resources.

Innovation Spillovers

The challenges of mining, refining, and manufacturing in zero gravity, vacuum, and extreme temperatures would require breakthroughs in robotics, autonomous systems, energy generation, and 3D printing using local materials. These technologies would almost certainly spill over into terrestrial industries—improving medicine, manufacturing, computing, and environmental management. Public and private investment in space resources would therefore serve as a force multiplier for U.S. R&D.

Reinterpreting and Modernizing the Legal Framework

Some legal scholars and policy experts argue that current treaties were never intended to ban resource extraction. The Outer Space Treaty prohibits national appropriation of celestial bodies—i.e., claiming sovereignty over the Moon or Mars—but does not clearly prohibit the taking and use of extracted materials. Unilateral action, in this view, is not a violation but an act of interpreting the law in a modern commercial context. The U.S. could use its actions to establish a new, more clearly defined legal precedent, effectively shaping future international law in its favor rather than being constrained by ambiguous rules.

National Security and Strategic Autonomy

Space is now a contested domain. By developing the ability to extract resources in space, the United States reduces its dependence on foreign critical minerals and rare-earth elements, many of which are currently controlled by China. In the event of geopolitical conflict, control over space-based fuel depots and raw materials would provide the U.S. with strategic leverage similar to naval control of sea lanes.

3. National Interests and Geopolitical Positioning

Unilateral resource exploitation is also framed as a matter of national survival and leadership in a competitive international system.

Preventing Adversaries from Setting the Rules

China has already landed on the far side of the Moon and has announced ambitious plans for lunar bases and asteroid exploration. Russia and China have signed bilateral agreements on lunar research. If the United States waits for a multilateral treaty, it may find itself operating under rules written by autocratic rivals. By moving unilaterally, the U.S. asserts its own standards and forces others to respond to its actions rather than the reverse.

Strengthening the Artemis Program and “America First” in Space

The Artemis Accords—a US-led set of principles for lunar exploration—already attempt to establish a framework for resource extraction that is favorable to U.S. interests. Some argue that the U.S. should go further and treat the Moon’s resources as part of the frontier spirit: not subject to international property rights but open to private claims recognized by American law. This aligns with domestic ideological values of free enterprise and could strengthen political support for NASA’s budget and missions.

Inspiring the Next Generation of STEM Talent

A bold, unilateral push into space resource extraction would be a source of national pride. Much like the Apollo program, it would motivate young Americans to pursue science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. The long-term benefit of a well-educated workforce is difficult to quantify but is often cited as a fundamental advantage of ambitious national space projects.

Avoiding a “Tragedy of the Commons”

Without clear ownership rules, space resources could be overexploited or, more realistically, no one would invest because no one can guarantee property rights. A unilateral U.S. policy would create enforceable property-like rights for American companies, incentivizing sustainable development and extraction. In this view, the U.S. is acting as a responsible manager of valuable frontier resources, similar to how European nations once opened the American West—though with modern legal and environmental safeguards.

Counterpoint and Final Thought

It is important to note that international law is not a trivial concern. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty prohibits national appropriation by claim of sovereignty. Many nations view any unilateral extraction without international consensus as illegal. Critics also argue that such a posture undermines the principle that space belongs to all humanity, risks diplomatic confrontations, and could trigger a space arms race.

However, the “supposed benefits” offered by advocates are clear: economic growth through a trillion-dollar resource economy; technological leadership through first-mover innovation and standards-setting; and national interests through reduced dependence on adversaries, geopolitical leverage, and domestic renewal. For many supporters, the greatest risk is not acting unilaterally—it is waiting.

Manifest Destiny Beyond the Sky: The Case for American Space Resource Dominance

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

In 1803, Thomas Jefferson nearly doubled the size of the United States with the Louisiana Purchase, an act many contemporaries considered constitutionally dubious and diplomatically aggressive. That single decision underwrote American prosperity for two centuries. Today, the United States faces an analogous inflection point — not across a continent, but across the cosmos. The Moon, Mars, and the asteroid belt contain resources of almost incomprehensible value: trillions of dollars in rare earth elements, platinum group metals, water ice, and helium-3. The question is not whether these resources will be claimed and exploited, but by whom, under what terms, and to whose benefit.

The United States should move decisively and unilaterally to establish ownership claims over extractable space resources, build the infrastructure to exploit them, and refuse to be constrained by international treaties — principally the 1967 Outer Space Treaty and the 1979 Moon Agreement — that were drafted in a different geopolitical era, reflect assumptions that no longer hold, and would effectively cede American advantage to rivals who have no intention of honoring those agreements themselves. This is not reckless imperialism. It is rational statecraft in a century where dominance of space will determine dominance on Earth.

I. The Treaty Framework Is Obsolete and Was Always Flawed

The cornerstone of international space law, the Outer Space Treaty (OST) of 1967, declares that outer space "shall be the province of all mankind" and that no nation may claim sovereignty over celestial bodies. The Moon Agreement of 1979 goes further, designating lunar resources as the "common heritage of mankind" and calling for an international regime to govern exploitation.

These treaties deserve scrutiny rather than reverence. The Outer Space Treaty was a Cold War instrument designed primarily to prevent the Soviet Union and the United States from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. Its language about space as the "province of all mankind" was aspirational rhetoric, not an operational legal framework. It contains no enforcement mechanism, no adjudicatory body, and no specific prohibition on resource extraction — only on national "appropriation" of celestial bodies themselves. The distinction between claiming sovereignty over the Moon and mining resources from the Moon is significant, and the treaty's drafters never envisioned a world in which private companies could land reusable rockets on asteroids.

The Moon Agreement is even less relevant. The United States never ratified it. Neither did Russia, China, or any other major spacefaring power. It has been ratified by only 18 nations, none of which possess meaningful space launch capability. To treat an agreement rejected by every country capable of reaching space as morally binding on American policy is not principled internationalism — it is unilateral disarmament dressed in legal language.

More fundamentally, the philosophical premise underlying these treaties — that resources in space belong to "all mankind" — is incoherent in practice. Resources that no one can access belong to no one. Value is not intrinsic to an asteroid drifting in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; value is created by the technological capability, capital investment, and human ingenuity required to reach it, extract its materials, and bring them to market. The United States and its private sector have invested hundreds of billions of dollars developing that capability. To declare that the fruits of that investment must be shared equally with nations that contributed nothing is not equity — it is expropriation.

The "common heritage of mankind" doctrine has a troubled track record even on Earth. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea attempted to apply a similar principle to deep-sea mining in the 1980s. The result was bureaucratic paralysis, a complex international authority that deterred investment, and decades of delay in exploiting seabed resources. The United States wisely refused to ratify that convention's deep-sea mining provisions. Replicating that model in space would guarantee the same outcome: resources left untouched while committees deliberate, and authoritarian regimes quietly building their own capabilities outside any framework.

II. The Economic Case Is Overwhelming

The economic potential of space resources dwarfs any terrestrial comparison. Consider the following:

Asteroid mining alone could be worth trillions. The asteroid 16 Psyche, which NASA is currently studying, is estimated to contain iron, nickel, and gold worth approximately $10,000 quadrillion at current market prices. While bringing that volume to market would obviously alter prices, even a fraction of asteroid-derived metals could reshape entire industries. Platinum group metals — essential for catalytic converters, electronics, hydrogen fuel cells, and medical devices — are scarce and expensive on Earth. A single 500-meter platinum-rich asteroid could contain more platinum than has ever been mined in human history.

Lunar resources are strategically essential. The Moon's south pole contains billions of tons of water ice, which can be split into hydrogen and oxygen — rocket fuel. Whoever controls lunar water controls the gas station of the inner solar system. A permanent American lunar fuel depot would reduce the cost of all deep-space missions by orders of magnitude, creating a cascading advantage that compounds over decades. Helium-3, abundant on the lunar surface and virtually nonexistent on Earth, is a potential fuel for fusion reactors. Should fusion power become viable — and billions are currently being invested in making it so — helium-3 could become the most valuable substance in the solar system.

Rare earth elements determine technological supremacy. China currently controls approximately 60% of rare earth mining and 90% of rare earth processing globally. These elements are essential for semiconductors, advanced magnets, electric vehicle batteries, wind turbines, and precision-guided munitions. American dependence on Chinese rare earth supply is a critical vulnerability that Beijing has already weaponized, restricting exports to Japan in 2010 and threatening restrictions against the United States. Space-derived rare earth elements would break this dependency entirely, repatriating a strategic supply chain and insulating American industry from geopolitical coercion.

The macroeconomic multiplier effects are historic. Every dollar NASA spent during the Apollo program generated an estimated $7-14 in economic activity through technology spinoffs, workforce development, and industrial capability. A national commitment to space resource exploitation would catalyze advances in robotics, autonomous systems, materials science, energy storage, life support systems, and propulsion technology — all of which have terrestrial applications worth hundreds of billions. It would create an entirely new industrial sector, generating millions of high-skill jobs in engineering, manufacturing, logistics, and operations. The first nation to establish a space-based resource economy will enjoy first-mover advantages that persist for generations, much as Britain's early industrialization underwrote its global dominance for a century and a half.

To share these benefits equally with the international community through some multilateral framework would be to socialize the costs borne by American taxpayers and entrepreneurs while distributing the returns to free riders. The American public has funded NASA to the tune of over $650 billion (inflation-adjusted) since the agency's founding. American companies — SpaceX, Blue Origin, Astrobotic, Planetary Resources' successors — have poured tens of billions more in private capital into space technology. No international treaty can justly require that the returns on these investments be communalized.

III. National Security Demands Space Supremacy

The national security argument for unilateral American control of space resources is not merely compelling — it is urgent.

China is not waiting for permission. The People's Republic of China has explicitly stated its intention to establish a permanent lunar base, exploit lunar resources, and dominate cislunar space. China's Chang'e program has already landed rovers on the far side of the Moon and returned lunar samples to Earth. The China National Space Administration has outlined plans for a crewed lunar base by the 2030s, with resource extraction as a stated objective. Beijing is not consulting the United Nations about whether the Moon belongs to "all mankind." It is building the capability to claim it.

China's 2015 national security law and its civil-military fusion doctrine mean that every Chinese space achievement is, by design, a military achievement. A Chinese lunar base is not a scientific outpost — it is a strategic installation. If China establishes resource extraction operations on the Moon before the United States, it will control access to lunar water, fuel production, and the high ground of cislunar space. The military implications are profound: whoever dominates cislunar space controls the orbital environment around Earth, including the satellite constellations upon which American military communications, navigation, and intelligence depend.

Russia, despite its economic constraints, remains a capable and hostile space actor. Moscow has announced cooperation with China on a joint lunar base and continues to develop anti-satellite weapons. The prospect of a Sino-Russian coalition controlling lunar resources and cislunar space while the United States defers to international legal norms is strategically catastrophic.

Space resources are military resources. Water ice is rocket fuel. Metals can be refined in space to build infrastructure, shielding, and eventually weapons platforms without the enormous cost of launching materials from Earth's gravity well. The nation that can manufacture in space from space-derived materials possesses an insurmountable military advantage in the space domain. In-space manufacturing also enables construction of large-scale solar power satellites that could beam energy to Earth or to forward-deployed military assets, and the construction of deep-space monitoring stations far more capable than anything in Earth orbit.

Deterrence requires capability and will. The Outer Space Treaty's prohibition on weapons of mass destruction in space is worth preserving. But conflating that narrow and sensible prohibition with a broader doctrine that space resources cannot be nationally claimed is a category error that weakens American deterrence. If the United States signals that it will not assert its interests in space for fear of violating the "spirit" of 1960s-era treaties, it invites aggression from powers that recognize no such constraints. Conversely, a United States that is actively building lunar infrastructure, mining asteroids, and establishing a permanent economic presence throughout the inner solar system presents adversaries with a fait accompli that raises the cost of competition and deters conflict.

The lesson of history is unambiguous: great powers that cede strategically vital domains to rivals in the name of multilateral idealism do not preserve peace — they invite predation. Britain's naval dominance preserved the Pax Britannica. American air and sea supremacy preserved the post-1945 order. Space supremacy will determine who writes the rules of the 21st and 22nd centuries.

IV. Unilateral Action Has Legal and Historical Precedent

The United States has already taken the first steps toward unilateral assertion of space resource rights, and those steps have been met with broad acceptance rather than crisis.

The Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015 (the "SPACE Act") explicitly grants American citizens the right to own, transport, use, and sell any space resource they obtain. This law does not claim sovereignty over celestial bodies — threading the needle of the Outer Space Treaty — but it unambiguously asserts that resources, once extracted, are private property under American law. The sky did not fall. No nation severed diplomatic relations. The international order did not collapse.

In 2020, the Artemis Accords extended this framework multilaterally, establishing principles for space resource utilization among partner nations. Over 40 countries have now signed, including major allies like the United Kingdom, Japan, Australia, Canada, France, and Germany. Notably, neither China nor Russia has signed — which means the Accords represent a coalition of the willing that already excludes America's principal adversaries. The framework is already bifurcated. Pretending otherwise is fantasy.

The historical precedents are instructive. The United States unilaterally declared the Truman Doctrine, the Monroe Doctrine, and freedom of navigation principles that became foundational to the international order. In each case, America acted first and invited others to follow. The result was not chaos but the establishment of norms that benefited both the United States and the broader international community. Unilateral American leadership in space resource exploitation would follow the same pattern: the United States establishes the framework, allies adopt it, and adversaries are presented with a reality they must accommodate.

Moreover, the principle that extraction creates ownership is deeply rooted in both common law and international practice. No nation claims that a fishing vessel operating in international waters must share its catch with all mankind. The fish in the sea, like the metals in an asteroid, become property upon capture. The doctrine of res nullius — that unowned things belong to whoever first takes possession — has a jurisprudential pedigree stretching back to Roman law. Applying it to space resources is not radical; it is natural.

V. The Moral Argument Favors Action, Not Abstention

Critics will argue that unilateral American exploitation of space resources is morally objectionable — that it constitutes a new colonialism, that it privileges the wealthy over the poor, and that it violates principles of global equity.

These objections fail on their own terms.

Space exploitation is not colonialism. Colonialism involved the subjugation of existing peoples, the theft of inhabited lands, and the destruction of existing societies. The Moon has no indigenous population. Asteroids have no inhabitants. There are no civilizations to displace, no peoples to oppress, no cultures to destroy. Conflating the mining of an uninhabited rock in the vacuum of space with the historic crimes of colonialism is not moral reasoning — it is moral posturing that trivializes genuine historical atrocities.

Inaction is not equity. If space resources remain unexploited because the international community cannot agree on a distribution framework — the most likely outcome of multilateral negotiation — then no one benefits. The rare earth elements remain locked in asteroids. The water ice remains frozen at the lunar poles. The potential for clean energy, technological advancement, and material abundance remains unrealized. A world in which American enterprise unlocks space resources and brings them to market is a world in which global commodity prices fall, clean energy technology advances, and material scarcity diminishes — outcomes that benefit developing nations far more than endless UN deliberation.

American prosperity radiates outward. The technologies developed for space resource exploitation will, as they always have, diffuse globally. GPS was a military technology; it now guides farmers' tractors in sub-Saharan Africa. Communications satellites were American innovations; they now connect billions in the developing world. The economic and technological benefits of American space leadership have never been confined to American borders, and they will not be in the future. The best way for the United States to benefit humanity is not to wait for a global consensus that will never arrive, but to lead — boldly, unilaterally, and unapologetically.

VI. The Cost of Inaction Is Unacceptable

The final and perhaps most powerful argument for unilateral American action is the cost of the alternative.

If the United States defers to international treaties and multilateral processes, one of two outcomes will follow. Either space resources will go unexploited for decades — a staggering waste of potential wealth that could address energy scarcity, resource depletion, and climate change — or they will be exploited by China, which has demonstrated no interest whatsoever in sharing the benefits with "all mankind."

A world in which China controls the resource economy of the inner solar system is a world in which Beijing possesses overwhelming leverage over the global economy and the military balance of power. It is a world in which American security depends on Chinese goodwill. It is a world in which the liberal international order — imperfect but infinitely preferable to any alternative — gives way to a Sinocentric system built on authoritarianism, surveillance, and coercion.

That future is not hypothetical. It is the trajectory we are currently on. China is investing massively in space capability. The United States is debating whether it has the right to mine the Moon. One of these approaches will prevail. The other will be studied as a cautionary tale.

Conclusion

The heavens are not a commons to be managed by committee. They are a frontier to be opened by those with the courage, capability, and vision to do so. The United States possesses all three. It possesses the most advanced space technology on Earth, the most dynamic private space industry in history, the deepest capital markets, and a legal and cultural tradition that rewards risk, innovation, and enterprise.

What it must now summon is the political will to act — to declare clearly that American citizens and companies have the right to exploit space resources, to invest massively in the infrastructure required to do so, to extend that framework to willing allies, and to refuse to be constrained by treaties that its principal adversaries ignore and that serve no interest but stagnation.

The Louisiana Purchase was criticized as overreach. The transcontinental railroad was called impossible. The Apollo program was deemed too expensive. In each case, the critics were silenced by the enormity of what American ambition achieved. The resources of the solar system represent the greatest economic opportunity in human history. The United States should seize it — not someday, not multilaterally, not tentatively, but now, decisively, and on its own terms.

The province of all mankind is best served when it has a leader. That leader should be — and must be — the United States of America.

OPINION: "Sharing" Space Resources — The Final Frontier of Bad Ideas

By Chip Flagworth, Fellow at the Institute for Manifest Destiny Studies

HOUSTON — Last week, at yet another international conference in Vienna, a man in a lanyard passionately argued that a nickel-iron asteroid 140 million miles from the nearest human being "belongs to all of humanity." He then returned to his complimentary hotel room, which very much did not belong to all of humanity, and ordered room service.

This is the state of the space commons debate in 2025, and honestly, it's never been funnier.

For those unfamiliar, a growing chorus of international law scholars, UN committee members, and people who describe themselves at parties as "space governance advocates" insist that the resources of space — trillions of dollars in rare minerals, water ice, and helium-3 — must be developed under a framework of shared international heritage. The practical result, naturally, is that they won't be developed at all, which I suspect is the actual point.

Let me be blunt: I support American companies going up there and mining space rocks. I think the Outer Space Treaty needs a robust reinterpretation. I think the 2015 Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act was one of the few things Congress got right that decade. And I think the "common heritage of mankind" doctrine, as applied to asteroids nobody has visited, is one of the most elegant mechanisms for ensuring paralysis ever devised by diplomats.

For expressing these views, I have been called a "cosmic colonialist," which I'm having printed on business cards.

But let's examine the opposition, because it genuinely deserves the satirical treatment its own internal contradictions invite.

THE TREATY THAT STOPPED A THOUSAND SHIPS

The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 is a remarkable document. Written when the most sophisticated thing we'd put on the Moon was a Soviet pennant that hit it at terminal velocity, it has been interpreted by critics of American space mining as a kind of celestial HOA agreement — one where 193 countries get to review your plans before you can touch a rock on an asteroid named 2011 UW158.

"The treaty clearly states that space is the province of all mankind," they say, with the confidence of someone who has definitely read Article II but skipped the fifty years of legal scholarship debating what it actually means.

Here's what's delightful: the same people who invoke the OST as sacred and inviolable are often the same people who'd like to replace it with something even more restrictive — the Moon Agreement of 1979. The Moon Agreement, you'll recall, was so popular that the United States, Russia, and China all declined to sign it. It is the international treaty equivalent of a party no one came to, and its supporters have been standing by the punch bowl ever since, insisting it's about to get going.

THE SHARING ECONOMY, BUT IN SPACE

The core argument of the "common heritage" camp goes roughly like this:

  1. Space resources belong to everyone.
  2. Therefore, no one can extract them without everyone's permission.
  3. Getting everyone's permission requires a comprehensive international framework.
  4. That framework will be developed through multilateral negotiations.
  5. Those negotiations are ongoing.
  6. They have been ongoing since 1979.
  7. They will continue to be ongoing.
  8. In the meantime, the asteroids will wait.

The asteroids, to be fair, are very patient.

What critics call "protecting the common heritage of mankind," I call "a process so slow that the Sun will enter its red giant phase before the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space issues a final permitting framework."

I recently attended a panel where a perfectly pleasant professor from a European university argued that asteroid mining should only proceed under a regime where profits are shared equitably among all nations. I asked him whether this model was inspired by any successful precedent. He mentioned the International Seabed Authority.

For those who don't follow the International Seabed Authority — and I assure you, nobody follows the International Seabed Authority — it is the body established under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea to manage deep-sea mining for the common benefit of humanity. It was created in 1994. In the thirty-one years since, the amount of deep-sea mining it has overseen for the common benefit of humanity is: none. Zero. An amount of mining indistinguishable from what would have occurred if the institution did not exist, because what has occurred is that the institution does not meaningfully function.

"But this time it'll be different," they say, "because it's space."

Ah, yes. Space. Famous for being easier to govern than the ocean floor.

THE COLONIALISM CARD

No discussion of space resources is complete without someone comparing asteroid mining to the Scramble for Africa, which is one of those analogies that sounds profound for exactly as long as you don't think about it.

The Scramble for Africa involved the violent subjugation of hundreds of millions of people who already lived there. Asteroid 16 Psyche has a population of zero. It has never had a population. It will never have a population that objects to mining because it is a lifeless metallic rock hurtling through the vacuum of space at 24 kilometers per second. The number of indigenous civilizations disrupted by mining it would be, and I cannot stress this enough, zero.

"But it sets a precedent," they argue.

Yes. The precedent of "going to a place where no one lives and doing something useful." History's greatest monster.

I want to be fair here, because the colonial analogy isn't made in bad faith by everyone who makes it. Some people are genuinely concerned about power asymmetries — the idea that only wealthy nations can access space resources, which would widen global inequality. This is a reasonable concern! I take it seriously!

But the proposed solution — ensuring that no one accesses space resources until everyone can — doesn't address inequality. It just adds scarcity to it. "We can't let Americans mine asteroids because Burkina Faso can't" is not the progressive argument people think it is, because Burkina Faso doesn't benefit from asteroids remaining unmined. Nobody benefits from resources that stay in the ground. Or in the vacuum. You know what I mean.

THE FREE RIDER'S GUIDE TO THE GALAXY

Here's a fun exercise: name the countries most vocally advocating for "shared benefits" from space resources.

Now name the countries actually building rockets.

Notice any differences?

I don't want to be crass about this, but there is something exquisite about nations that have invested precisely zero dollars in space mining infrastructure insisting on an equitable share of the proceeds. It's like someone who didn't chip in for pizza arguing about how the slices should be divided. Technically, you can make a moral case for it. But the guy who drove to the pizza place is going to look at you funny.

The United States has spent decades and hundreds of billions of dollars building the technological infrastructure to reach space. American companies — SpaceX, Blue Origin, AstroForge, and others — are spending billions more developing the actual capability to extract resources from asteroids and the Moon. The idea that the returns on this investment should be distributed through a UN body that will take forty years to agree on a font for its letterhead is not "equity." It's a mugging with better vocabulary.

WHAT I ACTUALLY BELIEVE (THE BORING PART)

Here's where I break satirical character slightly, because I think the debate deserves it.

I don't actually think international cooperation in space is stupid. The ISS is one of humanity's great achievements. I don't think treaties are worthless. The OST's prohibition on nuclear weapons in orbit is genuinely important. And I don't think the concerns about space becoming a lawless extraction zone are entirely meritless.

What I do think is that the perfect has become the enemy of the possible. We have a narrow window — maybe a few decades — where the economic case for space resource extraction will either be proven or abandoned. If we spend that window negotiating a comprehensive international framework that satisfies all 193 UN member states, we will negotiate until the window closes and then congratulate ourselves on our principled multilateralism while continuing to strip-mine Earth instead.

The Artemis Accords aren't perfect. The 2015 Space Act isn't perfect. But they represent an attempt to do something within a legal framework that allows for resource extraction while still honoring the OST's core principles. The alternative being offered — wait, study, convene, discuss, draft, redraft, ratify, implement, review — is not a serious policy. It is a elegant way of saying "no" while pretending to say "not yet."

CONCLUSION

To my friends in the "common heritage" camp, I say this with genuine affection: you are lovely people with beautiful ideals, and if the universe operated on the basis of what should be fair, you would be absolutely right. Space should belong to everyone. Resources should be shared equitably. International institutions should work efficiently and in good faith.

And I should have abs.

In the meantime, those asteroids aren't going to mine themselves, and I'd rather have an American company do it imperfectly under existing law than have nobody do it perfectly under a treaty that will be ratified approximately never.

Now if you'll excuse me, I need to update my business cards. I'm adding "Cosmic Colonialist" in Latin.
