"The Stars and Stripes Among the Stars"

A Speech on American Space Resource Leadership

Ladies and gentlemen, fellow Americans—

Let me ask you a simple question: Who built the rockets? Who spent sixty years, trillions of dollars, and the lives of brave astronauts pushing the boundaries of what humanity can achieve beyond this Earth?

We did.

And now—at the very moment when the resources of space are within reach, when the technology we pioneered can finally deliver unimaginable prosperity—we are told to wait. To ask permission. To defer to committees in Geneva and Vienna, to treaties drafted in 1967 when no one could actually reach these resources, negotiated during a Cold War by diplomats who couldn't have imagined a SpaceX Starship.

I'm here to tell you: the waiting is over.

I. The Opportunity Before Us

Above our heads—right now—there are riches that dwarf anything ever found on Earth.

A single metallic asteroid—just one, perhaps half a mile wide—can contain more platinum-group metals than have ever been mined in human history. We're talking trillions of dollars in cobalt, nickel, iron, rare earth elements, and platinum.

The Moon's south pole holds billions of tons of water ice—water that can be split into hydrogen and oxygen, creating rocket fuel depots that transform the economics of deep-space travel overnight.

Mars holds minerals, subsurface water, and the potential for entire new industries we haven't yet conceived.

These aren't fantasies. NASA has mapped them. Our private sector is engineering the tools to extract them. The science is settled. The engineering is ready. The only thing standing in our way is political timidity.

II. The Treaty That Time Forgot

Now, our critics will wave a piece of paper at us—the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. They'll tell us it says no nation can claim sovereignty over celestial bodies.

Let me be direct about this treaty.

It was written when the height of space technology was bolting a man to a tin can and hoping the parachutes opened. It was a product of Cold War anxiety—a mutual agreement between two superpowers to prevent nuclear weapons in orbit. A worthy goal for its time.

But here's what it doesn't do: it doesn't prohibit the extraction and use of resources. It doesn't define what "appropriation" means in the context of mining. It is silent on commercial activity because commercial space activity was inconceivable.

And the 1979 Moon Treaty—the one that tried to declare space the "common heritage of mankind" and establish international control? The United States never ratified it. Neither did Russia. Neither did China. It is binding on no major spacefaring power on Earth. It is a dead letter.

We are not bound by agreements we never signed. And we should not be paralyzed by ambiguity in agreements we signed for entirely different purposes.

Congress understood this when it passed the Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act of 2015, affirming that American citizens and companies have the right to own and sell space resources they extract. That was the beginning. But it was only the beginning.

III. If Not Us, Then Who?

Let me tell you what happens if the United States defers—if we wait for multilateral consensus, for a framework acceptable to 193 member states of the United Nations.

China doesn't wait.

China has announced plans for a permanent lunar base by the 2030s. They have mapped resource deposits. They are investing billions in heavy-lift launch vehicles with the explicit purpose of resource extraction. Their Chang'e program is not a science project—it is an industrial scouting mission.

Russia is partnering with China on the International Lunar Research Station—not with us, not under our framework, not under our values.

Do you think Beijing will pause its lunar mining operation to consult with the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space? Do you believe they'll submit environmental impact statements? Share revenues with developing nations who contributed nothing to getting there?

History answers this clearly: those who hesitate cede the frontier to those who don't.

When Spain and Portugal divided the New World between them at Tordesillas, England didn't recognize their authority—and England built an empire. When the great powers carved up Africa at the Berlin Conference, the nations that arrived first drew the boundaries.

I am not advocating colonialism. I am stating an iron law of history: resources go to those with the capability and the will to claim them. The only question is whether those resources will be claimed by a free society or an authoritarian one.

IV. The Economic Imperative

Let's talk about what's at stake at home.

America faces a national debt exceeding $34 trillion. Our infrastructure is aging. Our manufacturing base has eroded. We are dangerously dependent on adversarial nations for critical minerals—lithium, cobalt, rare earths—the very elements that power our technology, our electric vehicles, our defense systems.

Eighty percent of the world's rare earth processing is controlled by China. They have used this leverage before, restricting exports to Japan in 2010 over a territorial dispute. They can do it to us tomorrow.

Now imagine an alternative future:

American companies mining asteroids for platinum and rare earths, crashing the price of materials that currently give Beijing geopolitical leverage. Lunar water ice powering a cislunar economy—fuel depots, manufacturing platforms, tourism, research stations—all under American commercial leadership. New industries, new jobs, new tax revenue flowing not from debt but from the limitless wealth of space.

This is not a distant dream. The technology exists. The launch costs have plummeted—SpaceX has reduced the cost to orbit by a factor of twenty in fifteen years. We are on the edge of an economic transformation that makes the digital revolution look modest.

But only if we act. Only if we have the courage to lead.

V. A New Doctrine for a New Frontier

What I am proposing is simple and clear:

First: The United States should formally declare that space resources, once extracted, are the sovereign property of the entity that extracts them—American companies, protected by American law, backed by American power.

Second: We should establish physical presence and operational priority on the most resource-rich sites—the lunar south pole, near-Earth asteroids of highest value, Martian water deposits. Not paper claims. Operational presence. Infrastructure. Boots and machines on the ground.

Third: We should extend legal and, if necessary, security protections to American commercial operations in space, just as we protect American commerce on the seas and American interests abroad.

Fourth: We should invite allies—not adversaries, not the entire world, but trusted partners—to participate under American-led frameworks, like the Artemis Accords, which already have over thirty signatories. Those who share our values and contribute capability are welcome. Those who seek to obstruct or free-ride are not.

Fifth: We should dramatically increase public investment in space infrastructure—launch systems, in-space transportation, surface habitats, resource processing—treating this as what it is: the 21st century equivalent of the transcontinental railroad.

VI. Answering the Critics

I know what the objections will be.

"You'll start a space arms race."

I'll tell you what starts a race: weakness. Ambiguity. A vacuum of leadership that invites every nation to make its own rules. Clear American leadership, backed by demonstrated capability, stabilizes the environment. It deters conflict by removing any doubt about who sets the terms.

"Space belongs to all humanity."

A beautiful sentiment. The ocean floor also "belongs to all humanity" under the Law of the Sea. And you know what humanity has done with it? Nothing. Because when everything belongs to everyone, no one invests, no one risks, no one builds. Property rights and national initiative are what turn resources into prosperity. That is not greed—that is the lesson of all human progress.

"You'll damage international relationships."

Some relationships need to be re-examined. The international space governance framework was built for an era of two superpowers with ICBMs. Today we have dozens of spacefaring nations and private companies more capable than most national programs. The old framework isn't sacred—it's obsolete. We can build something better, and we will—but from a position of strength, with infrastructure already in place, not from a conference table where our ambitions are bargained away.

"It's too expensive."

The Louisiana Purchase was too expensive. Alaska was "Seward's Folly." The Apollo program consumed over 4% of the federal budget. Every great investment in America's future was called too expensive by those who lacked vision. The cost of not acting—of ceding the space economy to China—is incalculably greater.

VII. The Moral Case

Let me close with this.

There are those who frame this as selfishness—America grabbing resources for itself. I reject that framing entirely.

Throughout history, when America has led—when America has built, explored, invested, and yes, claimed—the world has benefited. American agricultural technology feeds billions. American medical research saves lives on every continent. American communications infrastructure connects the globe. American-led international orders, for all their imperfections, have delivered the longest period of great-power peace in human history.

When we extract resources from space, we will lower material costs worldwide. We will reduce the environmental destruction of terrestrial mining. We will generate technologies that benefit all of humanity—just as Apollo gave us water purification, CAT scans, and fire-resistant materials.

The question is not whether space resources will be used. They will be. The question is whether they will be used under the leadership of a nation that values freedom, rule of law, transparency, and shared prosperity—or under the leadership of those who do not.

I choose America. I will always choose America.

VIII. The Call

Two hundred and fifty years ago, a group of audacious men and women looked at a vast, uncharted continent and said: this is ours to build. They didn't ask permission from the old world. They built a new one.

Sixty years ago, an American president pointed at the Moon and said we would go—not because it was easy, but because it was hard. And we went. And we planted our flag. And the world watched in awe.

Now the frontier calls again. Larger. Richer. More consequential than anything before it.

The question for our generation is simple: Do we answer?

I say we do. I say we launch. I say we mine, we build, we settle, and we lead.

Not for empire. For prosperity. Not for domination. For security. Not against the world. For it—because the world needs someone to go first, and it has always been us.

Let the committees debate. Let the bureaucracies deliberate. America will fly.

Thank you, and God bless the United States of America.

Title: Seizing the Cosmic Frontier: The Imperative for U.S. Unilateral Action in Space Resource Exploitation

Introduction
Throughout history, nations that have dared to explore and dominate new frontiers have reaped unparalleled economic and strategic rewards. From the Age of Discovery to the Industrial Revolution, control over resources and territory has shaped global power dynamics. Today, the next frontier lies beyond Earth’s atmosphere: the Moon, Mars, and asteroids. These celestial bodies hold untold riches—rare minerals, water ice, and energy sources—that could revolutionize human civilization. However, outdated international treaties, such as the 1967 Outer Space Treaty (OST), which declares space as the “province of all mankind,” threaten to stifle American ambition. The United States must unilaterally claim ownership and exploit these resources, disregarding these constraints, to secure its economic supremacy, enhance national security, and lead humanity into a new era of prosperity.

Economic Supremacy: The Next Industrial Revolution
The economic potential of space resources is astronomical. Asteroids alone are estimated to contain trillions of dollars’ worth of platinum-group metals, while lunar regolith holds vital raw materials for space-based manufacturing. Water ice on the Moon and Mars can be converted into rocket fuel, drastically reducing the cost of interplanetary travel and enabling sustained human presence beyond Earth. By seizing these resources, the U.S. can catalyze a new industrial revolution, creating millions of high-tech jobs in aerospace engineering, robotics, and advanced manufacturing.

Private American companies like SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Planetary Resources are already pioneering these efforts, but their progress is hampered by the ambiguity of international law. Unilateral claims would provide the legal clarity and security needed to attract investment, spur innovation, and ensure that the U.S. remains the world’s leading economic power. If China or other rivals claim these resources first, the U.S. could face a catastrophic loss of economic leverage. By acting decisively, America can secure its position as the arbiter of the 21st-century economy, where space wealth flows primarily to U.S. shores.

National Security: Strategic Superiority in the Final Frontier
Space is no longer a distant dream—it is the next battlefield. Control over extraterrestrial resources directly translates to strategic military and technological dominance. A self-sustaining space economy would enable the U.S. to deploy and maintain satellites, stations, and defense systems without relying on Earth-based infrastructure. For instance, fuel mined on the Moon could power a network of orbital platforms, granting the U.S. unparalleled surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities.

Moreover, access to rare minerals like neodymium and dysprosium—critical for hypersonic missiles, radar systems, and advanced electronics—would reduce dependency on adversarial nations like China, which currently dominates Earth’s supply. Unilateral resource claims would also deter rivals by establishing a clear deterrent: any aggression against U.S. interests in space would be met with overwhelming technological and economic force. In an era where adversaries are rapidly advancing their space programs, the U.S. cannot afford the naivety of multilateralism that prioritizes idealism over survival.

Redefining the "Province of All Mankind": Rejecting Outdated Constraints
Critics will argue that the Outer Space Treaty prohibits national appropriation of celestial bodies, asserting that space should be a “common heritage of mankind.” However, this idealism is a relic of the Cold War era, designed to prevent conflict in an age when space exploration was nascent. Today, advancements in technology have rendered these constraints obsolete. The OST’s vague language fails to address the practical realities of resource exploitation, and its enforcement mechanisms are nonexistent.

Furthermore, the U.S. has a moral obligation to lead. By claiming and exploiting these resources, America can set the standard for responsible stewardship, ensuring that space development benefits humanity while securing its own interests. Other nations are already abandoning the OST’s principles: China’s lunar missions and Russia’s asteroid ambitions signal a growing disregard for multilateral norms. The U.S. must act before the skies are partitioned by rivals who care little for “shared prosperity.” History rewards the bold, not the passive.

Addressing Counterarguments: A Pragmatic Path Forward
Opponents may warn of international backlash or an arms race in space. Yet, the U.S. possesses the requisite technological and military might to deter any challenges. Moreover, by establishing clear precedents for space resource rights, America can shape international law in its favor, as it did with maritime and aviation standards. The 2015 U.S. Asteroids (Amendment) Act, which recognizes the right of citizens to extract and own space resources, is a critical first step.

The argument that space should be a “global commons” ignores human nature and history. Without the incentive of ownership, investment in space exploration and development will stagnate. U.S. leadership, conversely, will accelerate innovation, creating a multiplier effect that benefits all nations through technological spillovers and reduced launch costs.

Conclusion
The stars are within reach, but only for those bold enough to grasp them. The United States stands at the cusp of a cosmic renaissance, where economic power and national security are no longer confined to Earth. By unilaterally claiming and exploiting the resources of the Moon, Mars, and asteroids, America can secure its destiny as the preeminent global power for centuries to come. To hesitate is to surrender leadership to rivals and leave the fate of humanity’s future to chance. Let us seize the frontier, not as trespassers, but as stewards of a new era where U.S. ingenuity and resolve light the way for all mankind.
